prompt: Why does a reader have to read every line of a CSV file to get one column out of it?
hint: Where does the fifth field of the next line start?

choices.text: CSV files are always compressed, and compressed text is read whole
choices.why: The raw layer's CSV is plain text, and it was still read whole.

choices.text: Nothing in the file says where a field starts
choices.why: Right. Rows are written one after another, so a column can only be found by reading them.

choices.text: S3 only returns whole objects to Athena
choices.why: S3 serves ranges of an object; Parquet reads are ranges.

choices.text: Its header is at the end of the file
choices.why: The header is the first line, and it names columns without saying where they are.

prompt: Parquet with no compression at all took 24,667,617 bytes, against the CSV's 40,641,097, for the same orders. Where does that difference come from?
hint: How is a number written in each?

choices.text: Parquet left out the columns nobody queries
choices.why: Every column is there; the same totals came out of it.

choices.text: Numbers stored as numbers, and repeated words as a dictionary
choices.why: Right: four payment methods stored once each, with a small code per row.

choices.text: PyArrow compressed it anyway, with its default codec, despite the setting
choices.why: The layout asked for `none`, and Snappy took it down further, to 12,703,975.

choices.text: The 96 small files of each day share one footer
choices.why: That layout is the other one, and each of its files has a footer of its own.

prompt: Match each part of a columnar file to what it is.
hint: ORC uses other names for the same things.

pairs.right: A block of rows; ORC calls it a stripe
One column inside one group, compressed on its own
Where every block starts and what values it holds
Each repeated word stored once, with a code per row

right_distractors: A copy of the rows as text, for people to read

prompt: ORC with zstd came out smaller than Parquet with zstd. What should a lake make of that?
hint: Which decision mattered more?

choices.text: Move the whole lake to ORC, since ORC is always the smaller of the two formats
choices.why: This is one comparison on one dataset; the next dataset may go the other way.

choices.text: Keep both, so each engine reads the one it prefers
choices.why: Two copies of the curated layer is twice the storage and two jobs to keep in step.

choices.text: Little: both are good, and the decision that counted was columns over rows
choices.why: Right. Pick the one your tools default to and stay with it.

choices.text: ORC is smaller because it drops the footer
choices.why: ORC has a footer and stripe statistics too; the reader fetched its tail in five requests.

prompt: The gzipped CSV read 8,421,323 bytes, all of them, for a question about two columns. Why all?
hint: What did compression change, and what did it not?

choices.text: Compression shrank the read without making it selective
choices.why: Right: still every column of every row, just fewer bytes to fetch.

choices.text: Athena bills gzip files at their size once decompressed
choices.why: Athena bills the bytes read from S3, which are the compressed ones.

choices.text: ask.py cannot read a column of a gzipped file
choices.why: No reader can: the format, not the program, has no columns.

choices.text: The files were too small for the reader to skip any part
choices.why: A 40 MB CSV was read whole too; size was not the reason.

prompt: A source sends a single 10 GB export a night, compressed with gzip. Why does that slow a Spark job down, whatever its number of workers?
hint: Where does decompression have to start?

choices.text: Gzip is the slowest codec to decompress
choices.why: Speed is not it; ten workers would share a slow codec if they could.

choices.text: S3 limits a gzipped object to one reader at a time
choices.why: S3 serves any number of readers; the format is what forbids sharing.

choices.text: Workers cannot read CSV, only Parquet
choices.why: Spark reads CSV; lesson 17's script read the raw layer.

choices.text: A gzip file cannot be split, so one worker reads it all
choices.why: Right: decompression starts at the beginning, so the others wait.

prompt: zstd took the Parquet files from 24,667,617 bytes to 7,433,857, but the read for the payments question only from 6,481,669 to 4,280,951. Why did the read shrink less?
hint: Which columns hold most of what compression removes?

choices.text: zstd compresses less well on the second and later reads of the same file
choices.why: A file is compressed once, when written; reads do not change it.

choices.text: Its columns were small already; the savings lay elsewhere
choices.why: Right: `order_id` and `customer_id` shrank most, and the question touches neither.

choices.text: The footers are not compressed, and they are most of what is read
choices.why: The footers are a small part of either number; the columns are the difference.

choices.text: DuckDB decompresses before counting
choices.why: The count is of bytes read from S3, compressed.

prompt: A file compressed with ___ cannot be split: decompressing it starts at the first byte, so one reader takes the whole file.
hint: It is the codec the raw CSV was given.

prompt: The CSV month is 40,641,097 bytes and the Parquet month with zstd is 7,433,857. How many times smaller is the Parquet, to the nearest whole number?
hint: Divide the two.

prompt: What lets a reader skip a row group without reading it?
hint: It is in the footer.

choices.text: An index of every value, kept in the catalog
choices.why: The catalog knows partitions, not values.

choices.text: The smallest and largest value of each column chunk
choices.why: Right: a group whose largest hour is 20 cannot match `hour >= 21`.

choices.text: The row count of each group
choices.why: A count says how many rows, not which values.

choices.text: The partition key in the object's name
choices.why: That skips whole files; groups are inside one file.

prompt: The shuffled groups read 7,261,486 bytes for the late-evening question, more than the 4,914,494 of one group a day. Why worse than having no small groups at all?
hint: What did they skip, and what did they add?

choices.text: Shuffling broke the statistics, which are then ignored
choices.why: The statistics are correct, 7 to 23 in every group; they just exclude nothing.

choices.text: They skipped nothing and paid longer footers and worse compression
choices.why: Right: every group spans the whole day, and a jumble compresses worse than runs.

choices.text: A shuffled file has to be sorted again before it is read
choices.why: Nothing is sorted at read time.

choices.text: The shuffled layout has more rows
choices.why: Same rows, in another order.

prompt: The `groups` layout is sorted by hour. A query filters on `customer_id = 'c-17'`. How many of a day's twelve groups can the statistics skip?
hint: What range of customers does each group cover?

choices.text: Eleven, since one customer orders at one particular time of day
choices.why: Customers order at all hours, and the groups are cut by hour, not by customer.

choices.text: Most of them, since `c-17` sits near the very start of the alphabet
choices.why: Every group's range of ids starts near `c-1`, so `c-17` falls inside all of them.

choices.text: Almost none: every group spans nearly all the customer ids
choices.why: Right. Statistics help the column the rows are sorted by, and these are sorted by hour.

choices.text: All twelve, because the partition key is `dt`
choices.why: The partition skips other days; inside the day, nothing about `dt` helps.

prompt: In the sorted file of 15 October, how many of the twelve row groups have a largest hour of 21 or more, and so have to be read for `hour >= 21`?
hint: Read the right-hand column of `footer.py`.

prompt: Where should the sorting that makes row-group statistics useful happen?
hint: It costs nothing at query time.

choices.text: In each query, with an `ORDER BY` on the filtered column
choices.why: A query's `ORDER BY` sorts its answer, after the reading is done.

choices.text: In S3, which keeps objects sorted by key
choices.why: S3 orders keys, not the rows inside an object.

choices.text: In the catalog, as a property of the table
choices.why: A property describes; it rearranges no rows.

choices.text: In the job that writes the file
choices.why: Right: sorted once when written, skipped on every read after.

prompt: Why is `customer_id` a poor partition key for Quitanda's orders, though a question about one customer would open a single prefix?
hint: Count the files a month would leave.

choices.text: 39,979 tiny files, and nearly every question opens all of them
choices.why: Right: 318 bytes of data a file, less than a footer.

choices.text: A partition key cannot be a string
choices.why: `dt` is a string.

choices.text: The catalog refuses a table that has more than 10,000 partitions in it
choices.why: That is not the limit that matters; the free million is a hundred times further.

choices.text: Customer ids change whenever a customer moves house to a new address
choices.why: An opaque id does not move with an address.

prompt: On the small-files layout the month question read 27,000,299 bytes, more than the 22,068,273 the layout holds. How can a read exceed the files?
hint: How much does PyArrow fetch to find a footer?

choices.text: moto served each file twice by mistake
choices.why: moto served what was asked; the reader asked twice.

choices.text: Each file is under 64 KiB, so it was fetched whole, then its columns again
choices.why: Right: per-file overhead larger than the data it wraps.

choices.text: The listing of the 2,976 keys counts as bytes read, on top of the files
choices.why: The counter starts after the listing; only reads are counted.

choices.text: The 96 files of each day overlap, so that some of the orders are held twice
choices.why: The slices do not overlap; the same four rows came out.

prompt: Three years is 1,096 days. Kept as 96 files a day, read at two GET requests a file, how many requests does one question over all of it make?
hint: Days times files times two.

prompt: Which of these help against small files? Choose all that apply.
hint: Fewer, larger files.

choices.text: A compaction job that rewrites each closed day into few large files
choices.why: Yes.

choices.text: A coarser partition key, `dt` rather than `customer_id`
choices.why: Yes.

choices.text: A writer that writes one file per day, as `etl.py` does
choices.why: Yes.

choices.text: A per-query cutoff on the workgroup
choices.why: It stops a query; the files stay small.

choices.text: Smaller row groups inside each file
choices.why: That cuts files into more pieces, not fewer.

prompt: Which layout do the measurements recommend for Quitanda's curated orders?
hint: Both decisions, together.

choices.text: ORC partitioned by `customer_id`, the smallest files
choices.why: Small files are the problem, not the goal.

choices.text: Gzipped CSV by `dt`, which everybody can open
choices.why: It reads every column; that belongs in the raw layer.

choices.text: Parquet by `dt` and `hour`, written as 96 files a day
choices.why: That is the small-files line of the table.

choices.text: Parquet by `dt`, one file a day, sorted by hour
choices.why: Right, with zstd or Snappy.

prompt: Put these layouts in order of the bytes the month question read from them, most first.
hint: One columnar layout read more than the gzipped CSV.

prompt: A stream writes Quitanda's app clicks into `dt=` prefixes, one small file a minute, and analysts query them by day. What is the first fix?
hint: 1,440 files a day.

choices.text: Partition the clicks by minute as well, so that a query opens fewer files
choices.why: A day would still be 1,440 files, in 1,440 prefixes.

choices.text: A job that compacts each closed day into a few large Parquet files
choices.why: Right: the queries open a few files a day instead of 1,440.

choices.text: Raise the workgroup's cutoff so the queries stop failing
choices.why: They are slow and costly, not cut off; the files stay small.

choices.text: Write the clicks as CSV, so that every small file can simply be read whole
choices.why: Small files are read whole already; CSV removes what columns saved.
